Sanctions on Myanmar Electric Utilities Firms Disrupt Operations and Workforce

Sanctions imposed by the United States and European Union on Myanmar’s electric utilities sector have triggered immediate disruption across the industry, with several major firms reporting halted projects, suspended site operations, and mounting uncertainty for thousands of workers. The targeted measures, announced late Tuesday, freeze assets and prohibit transactions with Myanmar-based electric utility companies alleged to have ties to the country’s military leadership.

The sanctions have so far affected at least five of Myanmar’s largest electric utilities, including Eastern Grid Power Corp and Mandalay National Electric, according to statements from the Myanmar Electric Utilities Association. These companies collectively operate dozens of power generation and transmission sites nationwide. The association said in a statement Wednesday, “The sanctions have led to the immediate suspension of ongoing infrastructure upgrades and grid maintenance at several key facilities. Many sites are operating with only skeleton staff, while others have been temporarily shut down pending further guidance.”

Industry sources report that at least 4,000 workers—primarily technicians, engineers, and site maintenance crews—have been placed on indefinite leave. “Our members are deeply concerned about the abrupt loss of income and employment stability,” said Kyaw Thura, president of the Myanmar Electric Utilities Workers’ Union. “Many have been told not to report to work until further notice, but there is no clarity on when the situation may improve.”

The sanctions have also resulted in the freezing of company accounts and assets in foreign banks, severely restricting access to capital for maintenance and payroll. According to U Myint Zaw, a Yangon-based energy analyst, “Without access to international financial flows, electric utilities are struggling to pay staff and procure essential equipment. This could quickly erode operational capacity if the situation drags on.”

The Ministry of Electricity and Energy issued a statement urging the international community to reconsider the sanctions, stating that “the current measures are directly impacting the functioning of Myanmar’s electric utilities and pose risks to the livelihoods of thousands of employees.” The ministry called for “constructive engagement” to resolve the dispute.

As of Wednesday afternoon, site managers at several affected facilities reported ongoing security checks and restricted access to control rooms and substations. A senior official at Delta Electric Distribution, who requested anonymity, said, “We are prioritizing the safety of our staff and infrastructure while complying with government directives. Operations remain highly constrained.”

Industry observers warn that continued sanctions could lead to a deeper crisis for Myanmar’s electric utilities, with long-term implications for investment, employment, and the ability to maintain grid reliability. The situation remains fluid as stakeholders await further developments.
